evidence: Trax Records, founded in Chicago in 1984 by Larry Sherman after he bought the pressing plant Musical Products, released Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem)' in 1986. Jefferson also worked in A&R at the label. Trax was criticised for poor-quality pressings, partly on recycled vinyl, and for paying artists little, and several of its artists have disputed royalties and contracts (Wikipedia's articles on Trax and 'Acid Tracks').

later.title: Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem)

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen for the piano. Much early Chicago house was little more than drum machines and bass. 'Move Your Body' puts a rolling gospel piano on top of the machine beat, and it became the record that named the genre in its own subtitle. Then notice the sound quality of an original copy if you ever hear one: Trax pressed on cheap, sometimes recycled vinyl, and it can sound thin and noisy. The label spread house music fast and cheaply, and the artists paid for it.

explanation.age13: Trax was a small Chicago label that pressed many of the first house music records, including Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem)' in 1986. It made records cheaply, sometimes from recycled vinyl, and many of its artists say they were badly paid.
explanation.adult: Trax is the label through which much of early house reached the world, and also the standard example of how its artists were treated: cheap pressings, thin royalties and decades of disputes. Jefferson was both its artist and its A&R man, which is why the label edge and his production edge into Phuture belong together. The earlier side of the pair is the pressing plant rather than a record, because what the label shaped was how the music was made and sold, not how it sounded.
